explanation:
## How the rule was found

**What the grid is made of.** Every input has 3 rows, and each column holds exactly one grey (5) cell. The rest is background 0. In the output, some grey cells become green (3) and nothing else changes. So the rule only has to decide which columns get recoloured.

**Evidence from the changed cells (fact sheet):**
- Pair 1 (width 13): columns 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 change, which are the even columns.
- Pair 2 (width 12): columns 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 change, which are the odd columns.
- Pair 3 (width 14): columns 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13 change, which are the odd columns.
- Pair 4 (width 10): columns 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 change, which are the odd columns.

Read from the left edge, the parity flips between pairs. Read from the right edge, it never does. The last column always changes, then every second column moving left. Stated as a formula: a grey cell in column x turns green when (W − 1 − x) is even. Which row the grey cell sits in plays no part.

**Applying it to the test.** The test grid is 3×17, so W − 1 = 16 and the even columns 0, 2, …, 16 turn green. The odd columns stay grey.

**Construction stages.** The output starts as a copy of the input. The program then recolours, in one stage, every grey cell whose distance from the right edge is even, and emits that as the final canvas. The rule describes a single edit applied everywhere, so I emit only one stage.
